title: Attributive and substantival participles

objectives.can: Read a participle with the article as an adjective clause or as a noun ('the one who…').

explanation.summary: A participle with the article does the work of an English relative clause: ὁ πιστεύων is 'the one who believes'. Sometimes it stands alone as a noun; sometimes it describes a noun that is written beside it. Telling where the phrase begins and ends is the main skill.

sections.heading: The article turns a participle into a phrase about someone
body: You have met the participle's forms and you have seen an adjective with the article stand for a person or a thing. A participle can do the same. The article comes first, the participle follows, and together they name whoever or whatever does the action: ὁ πιστεύων in John 3:18 is 'the one who believes'.

The article and the participle agree in case, number and gender. The article therefore tells you the case of the whole phrase at once, and the gender and number tell you whom to supply: masculine singular 'the one who', feminine singular 'she who', neuter singular 'that which', masculine plural 'those who'. This is the same habit as in the lesson on adjectives used as nouns, now with a verb inside.

sections.heading: Two jobs: standing alone, or describing a noun
body: In the substantival use the phrase has no noun beside it. It is the subject, the object or whatever its case says: in John 12:44, ὁ πιστεύων is the subject of οὐ πιστεύει, and τὸν πέμψαντά με is the object of the preposition εἰς, 'the one who sent me'.

In the attributive use the participle describes a noun that is written. The usual form repeats the article: ὁ ἄρτος ὁ ζῶν in John 6:51 is 'the bread, the living one', that is, 'the living bread'. Another form places the whole participial phrase between the article and the noun: in John 5:37, ὁ πέμψας με πατήρ is 'the Father who sent me'. The two uses are close. What they share is the article, and that the participle describes someone or something already known in the sentence.

sections.heading: Where the phrase begins and ends
body: The article opens the phrase. Everything that belongs to the participle's action is part of it: its object, an adverb, a prepositional phrase. In John 5:24, ὁ τὸν λόγον μου ἀκούων is 'the one who hears my word'. The object τὸν λόγον μου stands between the article and the participle, and it is the participle's own object, not the verb's. The phrase is therefore as long as ὁ … ἀκούων.

Greek may also put the material after the participle: ὁ πιστεύων εἰς ἐμέ in John 12:44. A second participle linked by καί, with no article of its own, usually shares the first article: ὁ καταβαίνων … καὶ ζωὴν διδούς in John 6:33 describes one and the same subject.

The participle also keeps its verbal features. It has a tense and a voice, and it can have an object, as ἀκούων does. Its case belongs to the whole phrase and depends on the role of the phrase in the clause, not on the participle's object.

sections.heading: Tense and voice in these phrases
body: A present participle often names a person by something characteristic or continuing: ὁ πιστεύων, ὁ λέγων. An aorist participle often names a person by something that happened: ὁ πέμψας με, ὁ ἐλθών. These are tendencies. In this construction the tense forms present the action as it is seen, and the time reference comes from the whole context, so do not turn every aorist participle into an English past and every present participle into 'is …ing'.

Voice works as usual. τὸ γεγραμμένον in Luke 20:17 is a perfect passive, 'what is written' (the form stays the same whether you call it a perfect passive or the state it describes). τοὺς σῳζομένους in Acts 2:47 is a present passive: 'those who are being saved'. Neither passive tells you who the agent is.

sections.heading: What to ask when you meet article + participle
body: Ask four things in order. One: is there a noun beside it with the same case, number and gender (attributive), or not (substantival)? Two: where does the phrase end, counting the participle's own object and modifiers? Three: what is the phrase's case doing in the clause (subject, object, after a preposition)? Four: whom does its gender and number point to?
A participle without the article is a different matter: it usually adds a circumstance to the main verb, and the next lesson takes it up.

misunderstandings: Translating the article as 'the' and the participle as '-ing': 'the believing'. The natural reading is a clause, 'the one who believes'.

Treating the aorist participle as a mechanical past. ὁ πέμψας με is 'the one who sent me', but the aorist does not by itself decide the time of an action, and the present participle is not simply 'is …ing'.
Thinking a participle with the article needs a noun. When none is written, the phrase is the noun, and the article and the ending say whom to supply.
Cutting the phrase too short. The participle's object and modifiers stand with it, often between the article and the participle.

deeper.heading: Participle or relative clause?
body: Greek can say the same thing with a relative pronoun and a finite verb, 'the one who believes', or with the article and a participle. Grammarians point out that the participle phrase is the more compact and the more common of the two in the New Testament for characterising a person. The choice is a matter of style, not a difference of grammar that could be tested on a single word.
Whether a given present participle with the article names a general class ('whoever believes') or a particular person ('the one who is believing') is decided by the context, not by the form.

examples.analysis: ὁ πιστεύων is nominative singular masculine, a present active participle with the article: 'the one who believes', the subject of οὐ πιστεύει. τὸν πέμψαντά με is accusative singular masculine, an aorist active participle with the article, after the preposition εἰς: 'the one who sent me'. με is the participle's object.

examples.analysis: One long phrase: ὁ … ἀκούων καὶ πιστεύων, 'the one who hears and believes'. The participle's own object τὸν λόγον μου stands between the article and ἀκούων. The second participle πιστεύων has no article of its own and shares the first. τῷ πέμψαντί με is dative singular, the object of πιστεύων: 'the one who sent me'. The whole phrase is the subject of ἔχει.

examples.analysis: Here the participles describe a noun that is written. ὁ ἄρτος ὁ ζῶν repeats the article before the participle: 'the living bread'. Then ὁ … καταβάς, an aorist participle, adds a second description with its prepositional phrase ἐκ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ between the article and the participle: 'the one that came down from heaven'. Both agree with ἄρτος in case, number and gender.

options: Those who hear: masculine plural, a noun phrase
Hearing, as a noun for the activity

options: Nothing that belongs to the phrase
A second subject for the main verb
A prepositional phrase, ἐν αὐτῇ, which belongs to the participle: 'the things written in it'
practice.explain: The article τά opens the phrase and γεγραμμένα closes it. ἐν αὐτῇ tells where the things are written, so it belongs inside. The phrase is neuter plural, accusative: the object of τηροῦντες.

ὁ λέγων is the object of Ἔγνωκα

options: No: it is a finite verb
Yes: it is the subject of the sentence
No: without the article it is not a noun phrase here; it goes with ὁ λόγος as 'living is the word'
Yes: every participle means 'the one who …'
check.explain: The phrase 'the one who …' needs the article. Here Ζῶν is nominative singular masculine and agrees with λόγος; it stands first, which grammarians often read as a sign of emphasis, and it describes the word: 'living is the word of God'. Compare ὁ ἄρτος ὁ ζῶν, where the article is present.
